newsitem.title: CANADA: Gulf Canada moving top executives to Denver.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Canada moving top executives to Denver.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd., the Canadian oil and gas company that last year came under the control of Texan J.P. Bryan, said Wednesday it was moving its executive office to Denver from Calgary.
Gulf Canada said the move would give it better access to bigger capital markets and more international oil deals.

The move counters a trend that in the past year has seen several large companies such as Canadian Pacific Ltd. unit CP Rail and Suncor Inc., pull up stakes in eastern Canada and relocate to the Alberta city.

"We've made it pretty clear that we're going to expand internationally and the feeling among our leadership group is that being in Denver will help us do that without being all that far away from Calgary," Gulf's John Sparks said.
He said Calgary would remain Gulf's home base for North American operations. Gulf operates in Canada, the United States and Indonesia.
Under the plan, 20 of Gulf Canada's 25 corporate staff, including chief executive Bryan, will move to Denver by April 1, 1997.
But the company would remain a Canadian firm subject to the country's regulatory and reporting requirements.

Sparks said executives of Gulf Canada, whose predecessor company British American Oil was founded in Canada in 1906, spend much of their time with institutional investors in major U.S. cities such as New York, San Francisco and New Orleans. Denver is a logical hub, he said.

Bryan, a flamboyant Texan who gained control of struggling Gulf in 1995 with a C$300 million ($222 million) cash infusion, has said Canadian investment analysts have not given the company its due for opportunities created from his restructuring initiatives.
In the past two years, Gulf has trimmed staff, accelerated drilling, taken over smaller producers and restructured its debt. Financial results have progressively improved.
Bryan has said Gulf's troubled past, especially as part of the Reichmann family's ill-fated Olympia and York empire, made Canadian analysts wary of its stock, leading to lower prices than deserved.
